11210:
Imagine you are standing before a king. You lower your head, bend your body into a deep bow, and hold it there for a moment. That physical gesture — the bow — is an act of obeisance. It is something you do with your body to show a person (or thing) that you consider them far above you, that you deeply respect and submit to their authority or greatness.

Obeisance means a gesture of deep respect, submission, or homage directed toward someone or something of higher power or importance.

The word carries two senses that are brothers — one physical, one abstract.

1. The Physical Sense (a gesture)

This is the original and most literal meaning. Obeisance is a bodily act performed in front of someone to show reverence and submission. It is most classically a bow, a curtsy, or a full prostration (lying face-down on the ground). The key is that your body is physically lowering itself in the presence of another, which symbolises that you place them above you.

The knight dropped to one knee and made a slow obeisance before the queen.

The priests performed their obeisances at the altar before the ceremony began.

Notice that you do not just casually nod at someone as obeisance — it is a deliberate, formal, deep gesture. It carries weight and intention.

2. The Abstract Sense (an attitude of deference)

Over time, the word expanded beyond just the physical act. Obeisance can also mean the attitude or spirit of deep respect and submission itself — even when no bowing is physically happening. In this sense, it describes the way someone behaves toward a powerful person, idea, institution, or tradition, as though symbolically bowing before it.

The entire government paid obeisance to the old president's wishes, never daring to challenge him.

She refused to make obeisance to popular opinion and stuck firmly to her own views.

Here, nobody is physically bowing. But the spirit is the same — treating something as so powerful or important that you subordinate yourself before it.
The Three Things That Are Always Present

No matter which sense you use, three elements are always baked into the word:

Hierarchy — There is always a "higher" and a "lower." You show obeisance upward, never to an equal or to someone below you.

Submission — It is not just admiration. It carries a flavour of yielding, of placing yourself below the other.

Deliberateness — Obeisance is always a conscious act. It is performed on purpose, not accidental. You make or pay or do obeisance — it is something actively carried out.

Obeisance almost always appears in a small set of fixed phrases:

  • "make obeisance" — the most common phrasing, meaning to perform the gesture or act of submission.
  • "pay obeisance" — very similar; you pay obeisance the way you pay tribute, as an offering of respect.
  • "do obeisance" — slightly older-sounding, but means the same thing.

He bowed his head and made obeisance to the gods.
The citizens were expected to pay obeisance to the emperor during public processions.
The Register and Tone of the Word

This is important for a learner: obeisance is a formal, somewhat literary word. You will not hear it in everyday casual conversation. It appears in:

  • Literature and fiction, especially historical novels, fantasy, or anything with kings, emperors, or religious ceremonies.
  • Formal writing about politics, history, or religion.
  • Critical or ironic commentary, where a writer sarcastically accuses someone of bowing down to a powerful person or idea.

If you use it in speech, it signals that you are being deliberately elevated and formal in your expression.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are related but not identical:

Respect is broad and everyday. You can respect a friend, a teacher, a parent. Obeisance is narrower — it suggests a much bigger power gap and a formal, visible act of submission.

Reverence focuses on deep admiration and awe, often with a sacred or spiritual flavour. Obeisance focuses more on the subordination aspect — placing yourself below another.

Homage is very close to obeisance, but homage can also be something positive you offer freely (as in, "paying homage to a great artist"). Obeisance carries a slightly stronger sense of submission — of bowing down, not just honouring.

Deference is the abstract attitude of yielding to another's authority. Obeisance can carry this abstract meaning too, but it always has that physical, gesture-like quality lurking even in its abstract uses.

Think of obeisance as a word that captures the full picture of what happens when someone consciously places themselves below another — whether through a literal bow of the body, or through an attitude of complete submission and deference in behaviour. It is always formal, always intentional, always directed upward toward power, authority, or importance. The word carries a certain gravitas — even a theatrical quality — which is why it lives more in books and formal writing than in everyday speech.
11211: An obelisk is a tall, narrow, four-sided stone pillar that slowly gets thinner as it rises, and ends at the very top in a small pyramid shape. Think of it like a very tall, sharp pencil made of stone — wide at the base, narrow at the top, with all four sides gently sloping inward, and a tiny pointed pyramid sitting at the tip.

Every obelisk has a few defining features that make it instantly recognizable:

  • Four flat sides — each side is a flat, rectangular face
  • Tapered shape — it is widest at the bottom and gets gradually narrower going up
  • A pyramidal tip — the very top ends in a small pyramid shape; this pointed cap is called a pyramidion
  • Massive size — obelisks are typically very tall, often standing anywhere from 10 to over 30 meters high (roughly 30 to 100 feet)
  • Made from a single stone — traditionally, a true obelisk is carved out of one single, massive piece of rock (usually granite), which makes the engineering feat of building one all the more remarkable

Obelisks were invented and perfected by the ancient Egyptians, thousands of years ago. They were not just decorative objects — they held deep religious meaning. The Egyptians connected obelisks to the sun, and the shining pyramidion at the top was meant to catch the first rays of sunlight each morning, symbolizing the power of their sun god.

Obelisks were typically placed in pairs at the entrances of temples, standing like tall guardians on either side of the gateway. Their surfaces were often carved and inscribed with hieroglyphs — the picture-based writing system of ancient Egypt — recording the names of pharaohs and praising the gods.

Over the centuries, obelisks were taken out of Egypt by various empires — the Romans were especially fond of them — and transported to cities across the world. This is why today you can find ancient Egyptian obelisks standing in unexpected places far from Egypt.

Some of the most famous ones include:

  • Cleopatra's Needles — a pair of ancient Egyptian obelisks; one now stands in New York City's Central Park, and the other stands on the Embankment in London
  • The Lateran Obelisk in Rome — the tallest standing ancient obelisk in the world
  • The obelisk in St. Peter's Square, Vatican City

Many countries and cities have also built their own obelisks over the centuries, inspired by the Egyptian originals. Perhaps the most famous modern example is the Washington Monument in Washington, D.C. — while it is not an ancient Egyptian obelisk, it is built in the exact same shape and is considered an obelisk.

In everyday language, when someone says "obelisk," they almost always mean one of two things:

  1. An ancient Egyptian monument — a genuine carved stone pillar from ancient Egypt, or one inspired by that tradition
  2. Any tall, tapering, four-sided pillar built in that classic shape — even if it is modern and made of different materials

You might hear it used like this:

  • "The ancient obelisk towered over the entrance to the temple."
  • "The city erected an obelisk in the town square to honor its fallen soldiers."
  • "The Washington Monument is essentially a giant obelisk."

In a completely different context — the world of printing and writing — the word "obelisk" also refers to a typographical symbol: †. This small dagger-shaped symbol (also called a "dagger") is used in books and documents to mark a footnote or to indicate that a person is deceased. However, this meaning is far less common in everyday speech. When most people say "obelisk," they mean the stone pillar.
The core idea, in one sentence

An obelisk is a tall, four-sided stone pillar, narrowing upward and ending in a pyramid-shaped tip — a shape invented by ancient Egyptians as a religious monument and later adopted worldwide as a symbol of grandeur, commemoration, and architectural elegance.
11212:
Obese describes a person who has accumulated so much excess body fat that it poses a serious risk to their health. This is not simply a matter of looking "big" or carrying a few extra pounds. The word specifically signals that the amount of body fat has crossed a medical threshold — a point where the body is under real, measurable physical strain and where the risk of dangerous diseases rises significantly.

Think of it on a spectrum: a person can be slim, then average, then slightly overweight, and then — at a clearly more serious level — obese. It is not a vague or subjective word. It has a precise clinical definition.

Doctors measure obesity using a tool called the Body Mass Index (BMI), which is a number calculated from a person's height and weight. According to standard medical guidelines:

  • A BMI of 18.5–24.9 is considered normal/healthy.
  • A BMI of 25–29.9 is considered overweight (excess weight, but not yet at the obese level).
  • A BMI of 30 or higher is considered obese.

So, for example, a person who is 5 feet 9 inches (175 cm) tall and weighs around 203 pounds (92 kg) or more would have a BMI of 30, placing them in the "obese" category.

Doctors also recognize different levels of severity within obesity itself:

  • Class I obesity — BMI of 30 to 34.9 (the entry level)
  • Class II obesity — BMI of 35 to 39.9 (more serious)
  • Class III obesity (sometimes called severe or morbid obesity) — BMI of 40 or higher (the most dangerous level)
What Makes It Different From Just "Fat" or "Overweight"

These three words — fat, overweight, and obese — are often used carelessly, so it is worth understanding exactly how they differ.

Fat is a general, informal, everyday word. It simply means having a noticeable amount of body fat. It carries no specific medical measurement behind it. It can also be used as a rude or offensive word when directed at a person, even though it doesn't have to be.

Overweight means a person's weight is above the normal healthy range, but has not yet reached the obese threshold. It is a step above normal — a warning sign — but not yet at the level of serious health danger.

Obese is a formal, clinical, medical word. It means the person has gone beyond overweight and has entered a range where health is genuinely and measurably at risk. The key difference is severity and precision. A doctor calling a patient "obese" is not making a casual comment — they are making a specific clinical judgment based on measurable data.
The Health Consequences That Give the Word Its Weight

The reason "obese" exists as a special, separate medical category is because the health consequences at this level are well-documented and serious. Being obese is strongly linked to:

  • Type 2 diabetes (the body struggles to manage blood sugar)
  • Heart disease and stroke (the heart has to work much harder)
  • High blood pressure (the cardiovascular system is under extra strain)
  • Sleep apnea (breathing repeatedly stops during sleep)
  • Joint damage, especially in the knees and hips (excess weight crushes joints)
  • Certain cancers (including colon, breast, and liver cancer)
  • Mental health difficulties, including depression and anxiety

This is why doctors treat obesity as a medical condition requiring attention and care — not just a cosmetic or lifestyle matter.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Obese" is a formal, clinical, and neutral word in its intent. It belongs to the language of medicine, science, public health, and academic research. You will hear it from doctors, read it in health reports, and see it in government statistics. In those contexts, it is simply a precise, factual descriptor — no different from "diabetic" or "anemic."

However, in everyday social conversation, calling someone "obese" to their face — rather than in a clinical discussion — can feel cold, blunt, or even hurtful, because the word carries weight (in every sense). Many people are sensitive about their body size, and the word, while medically accurate, can land as harsh in informal settings. This does not make the word wrong or bad — it simply means that context matters. A doctor using it in a consultation is appropriate. A stranger using it as a comment is unkind.
How to Use It in a Sentence

Here are clear, natural examples:

  • "The patient was classified as obese based on his BMI of 33."
  • "The study found that obese adults are twice as likely to develop Type 2 diabetes."
  • "She was told by her doctor that, while not obese, she was overweight and should watch her diet."
  • "Public health campaigns have focused on reducing the number of obese children in the country."
  • "He had been obese most of his adult life, but after lifestyle changes, he lost enough weight to fall into the overweight category."

Since "obese" is the adjective, it is useful to know its family:

  • Obesity (noun) — the condition or state of being obese. "Obesity is a growing public health crisis."
  • Obese (adjective) — the describing word applied to a person. "She is obese."
  • Obesely (adverb) — very rarely used; in practice, you will almost never encounter this form.

The noun form "obesity" is actually used just as often as the adjective in real-world text, especially in news and health writing.

Obese is a formal medical adjective describing a person whose body fat has accumulated to a level — specifically, a BMI of 30 or above — that is measurably dangerous to their health and significantly raises their risk of serious diseases.
11213:
To obfuscate something means to make it deliberately unclear, confusing, or difficult to understand — usually to hide the truth or avoid giving a straight answer.

Think of it this way: imagine someone asking you a direct question, and instead of answering honestly, you respond with a long, tangled, roundabout answer full of vague words and unnecessary complexity — so much so that the other person walks away more confused than before. That is obfuscating.

The most important thing to understand about this word is that it almost always implies intent. When someone obfuscates, they are usually doing it on purpose. It is not just accidental confusion. There is a deliberate effort to cloud the truth, hide information, or make something simple seem complicated so that people can't see what's really going on.

The tone and feeling of the word. Obfuscate carries a strongly negative connotation. When you say someone is obfuscating, you are essentially accusing them of being dishonest, evasive, or manipulative — even if they never technically told a lie. It's a more sophisticated form of deception because the person is not making a false statement; they're just burying the truth under so much fog that it becomes invisible.
Where you'll see this word used in real life:

In politics: This is perhaps the most common place. A politician who is asked "Did you raise taxes?" might respond with a ten-minute speech about economic frameworks, historical precedents, and fiscal responsibility — without ever saying yes or no. That is textbook obfuscation. Journalists often accuse politicians of obfuscating when they dodge direct questions during interviews or debates.

In legal and corporate language: Long contracts and terms-of-service documents often obfuscate what a company is actually allowed to do with your data or money. The information is technically there, but it's buried in so much dense, complex language that the average person can't understand it. The complexity itself is the tool of obfuscation.

In academia and writing: Some writers obfuscate by using unnecessarily complicated jargon or abstract language when simpler words would do just fine. The result is writing that sounds impressive but communicates very little. A sentence like "The ontological underpinnings of relational epistemology necessitate a re-evaluation of subjective frameworks" might just be a very obfuscated way of saying "How we know things depends on our relationships."

In technology: Programmers sometimes deliberately obfuscate their source code — scrambling the structure and variable names so that the code still works but becomes nearly impossible for outsiders to read or copy. This is actually called "code obfuscation" and is a real technical practice.

In everyday life: Obfuscation happens in ordinary conversations too. Someone who is guilty of something might give a confusing, overly detailed account of their day to hide a simple fact. A company might bury a price increase inside a long announcement about "exciting changes." A person might use technical terms to make a basic mistake sound less obvious.
Example sentences to see it in action:

"The manager obfuscated the real reason for the layoffs by talking endlessly about market conditions and strategic realignment."

"His answer was so full of jargon that it only served to obfuscate the issue further."

"The report was deliberately written to obfuscate the company's environmental violations."

"She felt he was obfuscating, giving her every detail except the one she actually needed."

How it differs from similar words. Words like confuse, obscure, conceal, and mislead are all related, but obfuscate has a specific character of its own.

Confuse is more neutral and can be accidental — you might confuse someone without meaning to. But to obfuscate is almost always a deliberate act.

Obscure means to make something unclear or hard to see, and it can be used without implying intent. Fog obscures the road — the fog isn't trying to deceive anyone. But obfuscate nearly always implies a deliberate agent doing the obscuring.

Conceal means to simply hide something outright. Obfuscation is more subtle — the information may technically be present, but it's hidden within complexity, vagueness, or confusion, rather than being removed entirely.

Mislead means to point someone in the wrong direction, often by giving false information. Obfuscation doesn't necessarily involve false information — it works through confusion and overcomplication instead of outright falsehood. This is what makes it particularly sneaky.

The opposite of obfuscate. To do the opposite is to clarify, illuminate, simplify, or elucidate — to make something clear, transparent, and easy to understand.

The one-sentence test to know if you've truly understood this word: If someone is making something needlessly complicated, vague, or confusing — especially to hide the truth or avoid accountability — they are obfuscating. The fog they are creating is the tool, and confusion is the goal.
11214:
Obfuscation means the act of making something unclear, confusing, or difficult to understand. It refers to any process — whether done on purpose or by accident — that muddies, hides, or clouds something that could otherwise be straightforward.

Think of it this way: imagine you ask someone a simple yes-or-no question, and instead of answering, they respond with five minutes of complicated, roundabout, jargon-filled speech that leaves you more confused than before. That is obfuscation at work.
The two faces of obfuscation — deliberate vs. accidental

Obfuscation can happen in two ways, and understanding this distinction is key.

The first is deliberate obfuscation. This is when someone intentionally makes something hard to understand in order to deceive, hide the truth, protect a secret, or avoid accountability. A politician who is caught in a scandal and responds to every question with vague, tangled non-answers is deliberately using obfuscation as a tool of self-defense. A company that buries an important fee inside twelve pages of dense legal fine print is using obfuscation to stop you from noticing what you are agreeing to. In this deliberate sense, obfuscation is essentially a strategy of controlled confusion — the person doing it knows the truth perfectly well, but has chosen to wrap it in fog so that others cannot see it clearly.

The second is accidental obfuscation. This happens when someone makes something confusing not out of bad intent, but because of poor communication skills, excessive use of jargon, or simply not thinking about what the audience needs. A scientist who explains a simple concept using nothing but highly technical terms to a general audience is accidentally causing obfuscation. The intent may be perfectly honest, but the result is the same — confusion and a lack of understanding.

In everyday usage, the word leans more toward the deliberate kind, so when you see or hear "obfuscation," there is usually a subtle implication of intent behind it.
Where you will encounter this word

In politics and public life, obfuscation is extremely common. Politicians, press secretaries, and public relations professionals are often accused of it when they deflect questions, speak in circles, or use carefully chosen language designed to mean as little as possible while sounding like it means a lot. Phrases like "we remain committed to exploring all available strategic frameworks" instead of a direct answer are classic examples of political obfuscation.

In law and business, obfuscation appears in overly complicated contracts, terms of service, and legal documents that are technically readable but practically incomprehensible to ordinary people. The goal, deliberate or not, is the same: a reader who cannot understand what they are agreeing to is a reader who cannot push back on it.

In technology and computing, obfuscation has a specific and well-known meaning. Code obfuscation refers to the practice of deliberately rewriting software code in a way that makes it very difficult for others to read, understand, or copy — while still making sure it works perfectly. Developers sometimes do this to protect their intellectual property. Malicious hackers also use it to hide harmful code so that security tools cannot detect it easily.

In everyday conversation, you might use it more casually to describe anyone who seems to be making something harder to understand than it needs to be. "Stop with the obfuscation and just tell me what happened."

Obfuscation is not always an all-or-nothing thing. It exists on a spectrum. At the mild end, it might just be someone using slightly too much jargon. Further along, it is someone giving vague, evasive answers. At the extreme end, it is a fully calculated and sustained effort to completely hide the truth — through misdirection, overwhelming complexity, or deliberate misinformation layered so thick that the truth becomes almost impossible to find.

It helps to know what sits near this word so you do not confuse it with similar concepts.

Obfuscation is not the same as a lie. A lie replaces the truth with something false. Obfuscation does not necessarily introduce falsehoods — it simply buries, scrambles, or clouds the truth so deeply that it becomes inaccessible. You can obfuscate while saying nothing technically untrue, which is what makes it such a slippery and powerful tool.

Obfuscation is also not the same as simplification. Simplification takes something complex and makes it easier to understand. Obfuscation is the opposite direction entirely — it takes something (whether simple or complex) and makes it harder to grasp.

And it is different from ambiguity, though the two can overlap. Ambiguity means something could be interpreted in more than one way — it may be an accident of language. Obfuscation specifically refers to the act or process of making things unclear, with or without intent.

When someone accuses another person or organisation of obfuscation, it almost always carries a note of criticism. It signals frustration — the speaker feels that clarity is being withheld from them, either out of laziness, incompetence, or deliberate manipulation. It is not a neutral word. Calling something obfuscation is essentially saying: this should be clearer, and someone is responsible for the fact that it isn't.

Obfuscation is the act of making something murky, confusing, or hard to understand — whether to deceive, to protect something, or simply out of poor communication. It is the enemy of clarity and transparency. Wherever you see language, ideas, or information being made more complicated than they need to be, especially in a way that seems to benefit the person doing the complicating, you are likely looking at obfuscation.
11215:
If something is obfuscatory, it makes things harder to understand, see clearly, or figure out. It clouds, muddles, or hides the truth — like throwing a thick fog over something that could otherwise be seen plainly.

Think of it this way: imagine someone asks you a simple question — "Did you eat the last cookie?" — and instead of saying yes or no, you say, "Well, the concept of ownership over consumable goods in a shared domestic space is a philosophically complex one." That response is obfuscatory. It doesn't answer the question. It buries it.
The Critical Detail: It's Usually Deliberate

This is the most important thing to understand about this word. While something confusing might just be accidental — a bad teacher, a poorly written book — something obfuscatory carries a strong suggestion of intent. The confusion it creates is often on purpose.

When we call something obfuscatory, we are usually implying that someone is:

  • Hiding something they don't want you to see
  • Avoiding accountability or scrutiny
  • Making something appear more complex than it actually is, to manipulate or mislead you
  • Deflecting from a direct answer

This is what gives the word its sharp, somewhat accusatory edge. Calling something obfuscatory is not a neutral observation. It's a criticism. You are essentially saying: "This thing was designed to confuse you, and that was not an accident."

The word can describe a wide range of things:

  • Language / Writing: Legal contracts, corporate jargon, political speeches, and bureaucratic documents are frequently described as obfuscatory. They use dense, complicated language not because complexity is necessary, but because clarity would be inconvenient for the writer. A company hiding a fee inside 40 pages of fine print is using obfuscatory language.
  • Behaviour or tactics: A politician who never directly answers a journalist's question — changing the subject, going on long tangents, or reframing the question entirely — is engaging in obfuscatory behaviour.
  • Arguments or reasoning: If someone presents a deliberately tangled, unnecessarily complicated argument to avoid confronting a simple point, that argument is obfuscatory.
  • Design: Even a website or a form can be obfuscatory — for example, if a company buries the "cancel subscription" button behind seven confusing menus to stop you from finding it.
The Spectrum: How Obfuscatory Can It Be?

The word exists on a spectrum of intent and severity:

  • At the milder end, something obfuscatory might just be unnecessarily wordy or needlessly technical — more a sign of arrogance or poor communication than outright deception.
  • At the sharper end, something obfuscatory is a deliberate tool of manipulation, designed specifically to mislead, deceive, or prevent someone from understanding the truth.

Context usually tells you where on that spectrum something falls.

When something is described as obfuscatory, the person using the word is expressing a kind of intellectual frustration — the feeling of being deliberately kept in the dark, talked around, or treated as someone who shouldn't be given a straight answer. It implies a power imbalance: the obfuscator has information or a clear position, and is choosing not to share it plainly with you.
How It Differs From Similar Words

It's easy to confuse obfuscatory with other words. Here's how it stands apart:

  • Confusing is the broadest and most neutral term. A bad textbook is confusing, but not necessarily obfuscatory — it may just be poorly written, with no intent to mislead.
  • Vague means something lacks detail or precision. Vagueness can be innocent. Obfuscatory language can use vagueness as a tool, but it goes further — it actively works to prevent understanding.
  • Misleading focuses on leading you to a wrong conclusion. Obfuscatory language may not point you anywhere at all — it just stops you from finding the truth.
  • Evasive describes behaviour that avoids a direct response. Something obfuscatory is a tool used to be evasive — the means to that end.

Think of it this way: evasiveness is the goal, and obfuscatory language is often the weapon used to achieve it.

If you want a single sentence to anchor the meaning: Obfuscatory describes anything — language, behaviour, design, or argument — that is deliberately crafted to cloud understanding, obscure the truth, or prevent you from seeing something clearly.

The next time you read a contract full of impenetrable jargon, watch a politician dodge a direct question with a wall of words, or struggle to find a clear answer buried under layers of corporate-speak — you now have the perfect word for it.
11216:
An obituary is a written announcement that a person has died, published in a newspaper, magazine, or website. But it is much more than just a death announcement — it is a short biography of the person's life, written at the time of their death, so that the world can remember who they were.

Think of it this way: when someone dies, an obituary answers two questions at once — "When did they die?" and "Who were they when they were alive?"

A typical obituary includes:

  • The person's full name and sometimes a nickname they were known by
  • Their age and the date they died
  • A brief life story — where they were born, where they grew up, what they did for work, what they were passionate about
  • Their achievements — things they accomplished in life, awards, contributions to their community
  • Their family members — who they are survived by (spouse, children, siblings, grandchildren) and sometimes who died before them
  • Funeral or memorial service details — when and where people can come to pay their respects
  • Sometimes, the cause of death, though this is not always included
Who Writes It and Where It Appears

Obituaries are most commonly written by:

  • Journalists at newspapers, who write them for well-known or notable people
  • Family members, who write them for their loved ones and submit them to a local newspaper or funeral home website
  • Funeral homes, which often help families draft one

You will find obituaries in:

  • The pages of local and national newspapers (there is often a dedicated "Obituaries" section)
  • Online news websites
  • Funeral home websites
  • Community notice boards

An obituary serves several important purposes:

  1. It informs the community that someone has passed away, so friends, colleagues, and acquaintances who may not have heard the news can find out.
  2. It honors the person's life by highlighting their journey, personality, and legacy.
  3. It preserves their memory — obituaries are often saved by families as a permanent record, almost like a historical document of a person's existence.
  4. It invites people to mourn together by sharing the details of the funeral or memorial service.

Obituaries are written in a respectful, dignified, and warm tone. They focus on celebrating the person's life rather than dwelling on the sadness of their death. Even if the person had a difficult life, an obituary generally highlights the good — their kindness, their humor, their love for their family, their hard work.

Since you want a complete picture, it helps to know how an obituary differs from things that seem similar:

  • Death notice vs. obituary: A death notice is very short — just a sentence or two simply announcing that someone has died, often placed as a classified ad. An obituary is longer and tells the story of the person's life. Think of a death notice as a telegram and an obituary as a letter.
  • Eulogy vs. obituary: A eulogy is a speech delivered out loud at a funeral or memorial service, usually by a close friend or family member. An obituary is written and published for the general public. Both honor the deceased, but a eulogy is spoken and private (to those at the funeral), while an obituary is written and public.
  • Biography vs. obituary: A biography is a full, in-depth account of someone's life, often book-length. An obituary is a short, condensed version — essentially a mini-biography written specifically because the person has just died.

Here are examples to show you how the word is naturally used:

  • "I read her obituary in the newspaper this morning."
  • "His family asked the funeral home to help them write an obituary."
  • "The obituary described him as a devoted father and talented musician."
  • "She worked for years as an obituary writer at a local newspaper."
  • "The obituaries section is usually near the back of the newspaper."

The plural of obituary is simply obituaries.

  • "The newspaper published three obituaries on Tuesday."
  • "She flipped to the obituaries page every morning."

Obituaries are not only written for ordinary people — they are also written for famous individuals like presidents, scientists, artists, and athletes. When a very famous person dies, major newspapers like The New York Times or The Guardian publish long, detailed obituaries that can run for several pages. In fact, large newspapers keep pre-written obituaries ready for very old or ill celebrities, so they can publish them immediately when the person passes away. This is a normal journalistic practice and not considered disrespectful.

Also, the word obituary can occasionally be used figuratively — for example, someone might say "That was the obituary of our friendship," meaning the moment their friendship permanently ended. This usage is literary and not common in everyday speech, but you may encounter it in books or articles.

If you had to explain "obituary" to someone in a single sentence:

An obituary is a written tribute published when someone dies, combining the announcement of their death with a brief, respectful account of their life, so the world can know who they were and how to say goodbye.
11217:
To object means to express that you are against something — that you disagree with it, disapprove of it, or find it wrong, unfair, or unacceptable. The critical thing to understand is that objecting is not just a feeling you have privately inside your head. It is an act. When you object, you speak up, push back, or make your opposition visible in some way.

Think of it like this: you can dislike something and stay completely silent. But the moment you object, you have stepped forward and said, in some form: "No. I am against this."
The Word It Always Travels With

The verb "object" almost always comes paired with the preposition "to." You object to something.

  • She objected to the new policy.
  • He objected to being ignored.
  • They objected to the noise from the construction site.

You would never say "she objected the policy" — that is grammatically wrong. The "to" is essential. And notice the second example: when what follows is an action, you use "to" + the -ing form of the verb (to being ignored, not to be ignored).
Its Tone: Calm, Deliberate, and Often Formal

"Object" has a distinctly formal quality. It suggests that someone has thought something through and is choosing to register their opposition in a clear, deliberate way. It is not a word that carries rage or panic. It is measured.

This is precisely why it thrives in formal environments — courtrooms, professional meetings, official proceedings. When a lawyer shouts "Objection!" in a courtroom, they are formally declaring to the judge that a question or piece of evidence is inappropriate or inadmissible. That single word — rooted in this very verb — carries legal weight.

In a business meeting, someone who objects to a decision is not throwing a tantrum. They are calmly but firmly putting their disagreement on the table, often so it is acknowledged and recorded.
A Crucial Nuance: Objecting Is About Principle, Not Just Personal Discomfort

Here is something that separates "object" from many similar words: you can object to something that does not affect you at all. You can object on moral grounds, on principle, or on someone else's behalf.

A nurse, for example, might object to a hospital's policy not because it inconveniences them, but because they believe it is harmful to patients. A bystander might object to the way someone is being treated in a conversation they are not even part of. This gives "object" a slightly elevated, principled quality — it is often about what is right, not just what is comfortable.

This is important to understand: the verb says nothing about the outcome. You can object to something and be completely overruled. You can object loudly and be ignored entirely. The word only describes the act of expressing opposition — not whether it succeeds. So when someone says "I objected to the decision," they are telling you they spoke against it, not that they stopped it.
Silence Means You Are Not Objecting

The flip side of this is equally important. In many situations — formal meetings, legal processes, group decisions — if you do not object, it is assumed that you have agreed, or at least that you have no opposition. This is why you often hear phrases like:

"If no one objects, we will proceed."

The absence of objection is taken as acceptance. So the act of objecting is often the only way to place your disagreement on record.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how "object" differs from nearby words will sharpen your grasp of it considerably.

Disagree is milder and more conversational. You can disagree with someone quietly in your own mind, or in a relaxed back-and-forth. To object is more deliberate and carries more weight.

Oppose is broader and more sustained. You can oppose a government's foreign policy for a decade. Objecting is usually a specific, in-the-moment act — you object to this thing, right now.

Complain is focused on expressing dissatisfaction, usually about something that has affected you personally, and often with a tone of frustration or grievance. Objecting is more principled and less emotionally coloured.

Protest is louder, more passionate, and often collective. It implies strong emotion and sometimes public action — marches, demonstrations, vocal outrage. Objecting is quieter and more contained.
The Word Family You Will Encounter

Objection (noun) — the thing you raise when you object. "She raised an objection during the meeting." An objection is the statement or act of objecting itself.

Objectionable (adjective) — something that deserves to be objected to; something offensive, unacceptable, or morally troubling. "His behaviour was deeply objectionable."

Unobjectionable (adjective) — the opposite; something that is perfectly fine, that no reasonable person would object to. "The proposal was simple and unobjectionable."
Examples That Bring It All Together

• "Nobody objected when the deadline was extended — everyone was relieved."
  • "She strongly objected to being described as careless."
  • "The committee objected to the proposed budget cuts."
  • "I object to the tone you are using in this conversation."
  • "He objected on moral grounds, even though the decision didn't affect him directly."
  • "She did not object, so we assumed she was fine with the plan."
The Single Cleanest Way to Remember It

If you ever need to recall this word in a flash, hold onto this: to object is to stand up and say "I am against this." It is formal, deliberate, principled, and always directed at something specific. It is about the act of speaking your opposition — regardless of whether anyone listens, and regardless of whether it changes anything.
11218:
To objectify someone means to treat them as an object — as a thing — rather than as a full human being.

When you objectify a person, you stop seeing them as someone with feelings, thoughts, desires, and inner life. Instead, you see them only in terms of what they look like, what they can do for you, or what purpose they serve. You reduce them from a who to a what.

Here is a simple way to feel this contrast: objects don't have feelings. A chair doesn't care how you treat it. A car has no personality, no fears, no dreams. When you objectify a person, you mentally — and often behaviorally — treat them the same way. As something to be used, viewed, evaluated, or consumed, rather than someone to be respected, listened to, and understood.
The most common use: sexual objectification

The word is most frequently used in the context of attraction and sexuality. To sexually objectify someone means to focus only on their body or physical appearance, as if that is the only thing about them that has any value, while completely ignoring their personality, intelligence, feelings, and humanity.

A person who stares at someone and thinks purely about their body, with zero curiosity about who they are, is objectifying them. Advertisements that use a woman's body to sell a product — treating her body as decoration or bait — objectify her. Comments that reduce a person to their physical features objectify them. The harm is not just psychological; it sends a message to people that they exist to be looked at or used, not known or valued.
The broader sense: treating people as tools

Beyond sexuality, the word applies to any situation where a person is treated purely as a means to an end — as an instrument rather than a human being.

A manager who sees employees only as units of productivity, with no interest in their wellbeing, is objectifying them. Someone who befriends another person only to use their wealth or connections, caring nothing about them personally, is objectifying them. Slavery is one of history's most extreme forms of objectification — human beings legally treated as property, as things to be bought, sold, and used. In all of these cases, the same thing is being erased: the person's full humanity.
What exactly gets taken away when someone is objectified

Objectification works by mentally removing or ignoring the things that make someone a person rather than a thing. Specifically:

Their feelings are ignored — objects don't hurt, so the objectified person's emotional experience doesn't register as important. Their autonomy is denied — objects don't get to make choices, so the person's right to decide things for themselves is disregarded or overridden. Their individuality is erased — objects are interchangeable, so the person is treated as replaceable, one of many, not unique. Their inherent dignity and worth are stripped — objects have value only in how useful or pleasing they are, so the person is valued only for what they offer, not for simply being.

In formal or philosophical writing, "objectify" can also mean to give a concrete, visible, or tangible form to something abstract or internal.

For example: "The painting objectifies her loneliness." This means the artist has taken an invisible inner experience — loneliness — and given it a concrete, external form you can see. This use is legitimate but much rarer. You are unlikely to encounter it in everyday conversation.

Objectification is the noun — the act or result of objectifying. "The objectification of women in advertising is widely criticized." Objectified is the past tense and is also used as an adjective. "She felt objectified by the remark." Objectifying is the present participle. "That kind of language is objectifying."
The one sentence that holds it all together
To objectify is to mentally delete the personhood from a human being and interact with what remains — a body, a tool, a thing — as if that partial picture were the whole truth of who they are.
11219:
An objection is a reason you give — or a statement you make — to express that you disagree with, disapprove of, or have a problem with something.

It is not just a simple "no." An objection implies that you have grounds — a basis, a concern, a reason — for your disagreement. You are not just refusing; you are pushing back with some justification.

Think of it this way: when someone proposes a plan, a rule, an argument, or an action, and you say "Wait — I think there is a problem with this, and here is why" — that reasoning and pushback is your objection.

An objection always involves three elements:

  1. Something being said, proposed, or done — a claim, a plan, a decision, a question, an action.
  2. Someone who disagrees — they find a flaw, a problem, an unfairness, or a conflict with their values.
  3. The expression of that disagreement, with a reason — this expression, this voiced concern, is the objection itself.
How It Is Used in Everyday Life

In ordinary conversation, an objection is simply a concern or disagreement someone raises.

  • "Does anyone have any objections to meeting on Friday?" — Is anyone against it? Does anyone have a problem with it?
  • "My main objection to the plan is that it costs too much." — The primary reason I disagree is the cost.
  • "She raised an objection during the meeting." — She spoke up to express a disagreement or concern.
  • "I have no objection to that." — I am perfectly fine with it; I do not disagree.

Notice how in each case, the objection is tied to a reason or a concern, not just a feeling of dislike.

This is perhaps the setting where the word is most dramatically used, and it has a very specific meaning here.

During a trial, a lawyer can say "Objection!" to formally protest to the judge that something happening in the courtroom is improper. The "something" could be:

  • A question the other lawyer asked a witness (perhaps it is misleading, irrelevant, or assumes facts not in evidence).
  • A piece of evidence being presented improperly.
  • A procedure not being followed correctly.

The judge then makes a decision:

  • "Sustained" — The judge agrees with the objection. The improper action is stopped.
  • "Overruled" — The judge disagrees with the objection. The action is allowed to continue.

So in law, an objection is a formal, on-the-record protest that something violates the rules of the court.

When people discuss ideas, theories, or positions — in philosophy, academics, or even serious debates — an objection is a counterargument raised against a claim.

For example, if someone argues "We should work longer hours to be more productive," an objection might be: "But research shows that overwork leads to burnout and actually reduces long-term productivity."

Here, the objection challenges the original argument by pointing out a flaw, a contradiction, or a piece of evidence that weakens it. It is a tool of critical thinking — a way of testing whether an idea holds up under scrutiny.

An objection can also come from deep personal, moral, or religious beliefs.

  • A doctor might have a moral objection to performing a certain procedure because it conflicts with their ethics.
  • A soldier might have a conscientious objection to fighting in a war — meaning they refuse on the grounds of deep moral or religious belief. (A person who does this is called a conscientious objector.)

Here, the objection is not an intellectual counterargument but a principled, values-based refusal or protest.

Objections are not all equal. They can vary in weight and seriousness:

  • A minor objection — a small concern that can perhaps be addressed easily. "My only objection is the font size — it is too small."
  • A serious / strong objection — a major concern that fundamentally challenges something. "I have serious objections to the entire approach."
  • A fundamental objection — one that goes to the very heart of the matter, questioning the whole idea rather than just a detail.
Key Phrases and Expressions You Will Encounter

Raise an objection — to bring up or voice a concern formally or semi-formally. "He raised several objections during the discussion."

Voice an objection — similar to "raise," but with a slight emphasis on speaking up. "She voiced her objections clearly."

Have no objection — to be fine with something, to agree or accept it. "I have no objection to the proposal."

Object to something — the verb form; it means to express an objection. "She objected to the new policy."

Overrule an objection — (mainly legal) to reject the objection as invalid.

Sustain an objection — (mainly legal) to accept the objection as valid.

File an objection — (legal/formal) to submit an objection officially as a document.

Meet an objection — to address and respond to an objection, usually by explaining why it is not valid. "The manager met every objection with a clear answer."

An objection is generally a rational, reasoned form of disagreement. It sits somewhere between a casual doubt and a full refusal. It says:

"I am not simply ignoring this. I am engaging with it, and I am telling you specifically what the problem is."

Because it carries a reason with it, an objection invites dialogue. Unlike a flat refusal, it opens the door to discussion — the other side can try to answer the objection, and if they do so successfully, the objection may be withdrawn.

An objection is a stated reason for disagreeing with or opposing something. It can arise in:

  • Everyday situations — any time someone has a concern or disagreement with a plan, decision, or statement.
  • Legal settings — a formal protest by a lawyer that something is improper.
  • Intellectual debates — a counterargument that challenges a claim or theory.
  • Moral or personal contexts — a principled refusal based on values or beliefs.

An objection always says: "I disagree, and here is why." That "here is why" is what makes it an objection, rather than just a refusal or a complaint.
